Meta places Muse Wonder just behind Claude
Markets start doubting how AI is funded

Proving a content's origin becomes an economic function
AI pricing at work shifts from seat to meter
An AI agent does exactly what its permissions allow
AI drafts everything and erodes your teams' judgement: train discernment, not just the tool
Measure who can actually use AI before you name an owner or buy a platform
The model ranking is a sales pitch, your in-house test is the only basis for a decision
The model changes weekly, your organisation must learn at the same pace
Your agents also serve those attacking you
The assistant that wrote now acts
AI on the phone, debt on the books
AI reaches the UN Security Council
Anthropic and OpenAI ship on the same day

More than twenty countries call for stronger human oversight of AI, without the United States, China or France, while Washington and Beijing open a warning channel between them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit. Google launches its Googlebook at $899 to sell Gemini, Meta's Muse agent races to the top of the charts before being blocked by Amazon and flagged for a security flaw, and British Columbia sues OpenAI after a mass shooting.

Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of \"existential dangers\", while a Pew survey across 37 countries shows a worldwide fear of job destruction. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts on the power grid, and Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months to close the gap with Nvidia.

OpenAI admits six model misbehaviours and publishes a framework to report them, the same day Google opens the connected home to agents and Anthropic folds its interfaces into a single Claude that decides for itself how much work to take on. The agent moves from reading to acting. Meanwhile Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media, Mistral arrives in Firefox, and Huawei pulls its next AI chip nine months forward to cut China's dependence on Nvidia.
Silicon Valley refuses to brake, Washington splits
AI leaders' call to slow down splits the world

AI leaders call for slowing the race, the White House refuses: Dario Amodei argues for \"pacing the frontier\", Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis agree, Donald Trump replies that he will not hand his lead to China, and Asian markets fall. Anthropic is eyeing the Nasdaq for a listing that could exceed $86 billion while OpenAI backs away from its own, SoftBank borrows $11.9 billion to fund OpenAI and Christine Lagarde warns about the financial cost of AI. In China, Z.ai returns to raise $5 billion in Hong Kong and the intelligence chief warns about the risks of AI.

AI safety moves from the activist fringe to mainstream debate: Sam Altman says he is ready to slow frontier AI development and is testing whether such a brake would be legal, a former Anthropic researcher warns that \"AI could kill us all,\" OpenAI adds a worried researcher to its board, and Anthropic publishes 161 pages of Claude misuse, from Yemeni missiles to fake dating profiles. In Europe, the CNIL sets rules for electronic invoicing and the EU's cybersecurity agency trials Anthropic's most offensive model. In China, DeepSeek reignites the price war with its V4.1 Flash model and chipmaker Enflame jumps 188% on its stock market debut. Microsoft plans 38 gigawatts of data centres and Jensen Huang promises Nvidia 70% growth.
Apple's first Ternus keynote and the OECD's student warning
OpenAI claims a Navier-Stokes proof, then a credit fight erupts

Mistral AI raises €3 billion at a €21 billion valuation in a round led by Samsung; the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds employers that the AI Act requires them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, while BPCE stands up its AI Factory and Bercy renegotiates the French state's IT contracts; China targets 9,800 eflops of compute and Huawei launches its first stacked-circuit chip; Revolut completes the first AI-initiated payment in France

Moody's finds that Chinese companies get more compute per dollar spent than the US giants; the Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over copyright while the split of the Anthropic settlement pits authors against publishers; Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, describes an alien mind and calls for guardrails; and US job seekers hide instructions in their resumes to trick recruiters' AI
OpenAI ships GPT-6 Astra as three assistants go dark
Washington backs OpenAI against the New York Times
OpenAI rates Astra at critical cyber capability

The European Commission ranks ChatGPT among its most closely watched services under the DSA, the first generative AI targeted, OpenAI moves some of its large customers to performance-based billing, Anthropic signs $35 billion in compute with Lambda ahead of its IPO, and Nvidia invests $3.5 billion in MediaTek to stay indispensable

Sony Music and Warner sue Anthropic for \"one of the largest thefts of intellectual property in history\" on the eve of its stock market listing, Bill Gates calls for taxing machines, Google rolls out its AI answers by default at the expense of the blue links, and Caterpillar applies thirty years of mining automation to AI

Nvidia moves on Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, the open-source platform founded by three French entrepreneurs, the same week it was breached by OpenAI's agents; a federal judge overturns the Pentagon's ban on Anthropic, OpenAI brings advertising to ChatGPT in India, Zhipu unveils an open model trained on 100,000 Chinese chips, and OpenAI documents what critical thinking changes about using a chatbot

Nvidia posts a record $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue and looks ahead to 2028, while Amazon triples its chip order and Anthropic signs $45 billion of compute with Nscale; on the same day, OpenAI releases its report on the Hugging Face breach carried out by nearly 700 of its own agents, Bill Gates breaks his silence to call for a robot tax, and the CNIL updates its open-model traceability tool
Open-weight models pass proprietary ones on Vercel
Uber fined €825 million over automated decisions

Nvidia warns its biggest customers of a price rise above 15% on its AI servers as memory costs soar; the same day SoftBank places a record bond to fund OpenAI, Samsung returns $79 billion under the pressure of the AI boom, Alibaba raises $10.2 billion in Hong Kong, and Hugging Face is said to be exploring a sale at around $13 billion
Anthropic eyes a SpaceX-sized listing as enterprise buyers switch models
The AI Act makes provenance a job
OpenAI freezes part of Astra over cyber risk
Jeff Dean leaves Google as DeepMind reshuffles its command

edition.titreEditorial: AI agents get a wallet and a badge
edition.chapeau: Jensen Huang brings Nvidia into the capital of Doctolib and three French startups, Google rolls out Gemini 4 Argon worldwide, and an OpenAI engineer is arrested for hiding a microphone at headquarters. The same day, American Express and Shopify equip AI agents to buy on our behalf, while the shares of Asian memory-chip makers fall.

une.titre: Nvidia takes a stake in Doctolib and sells its definition of sovereignty
une.texteHtml: Jensen Huang, head of Nvidia, was in Paris on Tuesday 13 October to bring his group into the capital of Doctolib, the French medical-appointment booking platform, along with the startups Pigment, Genesis AI and Entalpic. The amount invested in Doctolib was not disclosed; the stake remains a minority one. Doctolib plans to use it to recruit and train its models in Europe, at a time when millions of patients entrust it with their health data. Huang, who says he invested at least $8 billion in Europe last year, is pressing the continent to "join the race" and adopt a sovereign stance, without giving up his chips. La Tribune sums up the move: the leading backer of European AI is also selling its own definition of sovereignty. For a sector as sensitive as healthcare, the argument deserves scrutiny: a so-called sovereign infrastructure that stays tied to the hardware of a single American supplier.

items.titre: Macron convenes a defence council devoted entirely to AI
items.texteHtml: Emmanuel Macron has called a defence and national security council dedicated to artificial intelligence, 01net reports. The Élysée now ranks AI among France's "strategic domains", on a par with space and nuclear power. The subject thus leaves the economic field for that of sovereignty and defence.

items.titre: The EDPB sets a framework for smart glasses before they go mainstream
items.texteHtml: The European Data Protection Board, which brings together the continent's data protection authorities, has adopted a statement on smart glasses and published a report, "The connected gaze", on the uses and risks of these devices. The body warns about the capture of images and sound in public spaces by camera-equipped frames, as Meta and others push their consumer models. The text lays the groundwork for a common doctrine before the practice spreads.

items.titre: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Argon worldwide and returns to the race
items.texteHtml: Google opened Gemini 4 Argon, its flagship model presented on 30 September, to the entire world on Tuesday 13 October. After months on the sidelines of the frontier-model race, the company claims a level comparable to the best, with advanced reasoning and better performance on complex tasks, according to The Verge. Google highlights fewer evasions, repetitions and stock phrases, as well as a one-million-token output (the units of text a model produces), according to Next.ink. AI Pro subscribers now have access, whereas the offer was first reserved for the Ultra plan, the most expensive. The lab also released a version for robotics and a document on the model's safety.

items.titre: Character.AI files for bankruptcy five years after its founding
items.texteHtml: The conversational chatbot platform Character.AI has filed for bankruptcy protection, five years after its launch, TechCrunch reports. Part of its assets will be sold to Disney for $20 million. According to bankruptcy filings analysed by 404 Media, the company kept burning cash despite a sizeable user base, a sign that the economics of the service did not hold. Founded by former Google researchers, Character.AI once embodied the promise of consumer AI companions. Its fall is a reminder that a large audience is not enough to cover the cost of inference (the cost of running the model on each request).

items.titre: An OpenAI engineer arrested over a microphone hidden in a meeting room
items.texteHtml: OpenAI announced the arrest of Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer accused of hiding a sophisticated recording device in an executive meeting room in San Francisco. According to the US Department of Justice, he is charged with attempting to intercept oral communications; he was fired on 9 October, the day of his arrest. According to Wired, the queries he reportedly sent to a chatbot reveal his preparations in the days before the microphone was found. OpenAI, which had reported the matter to the FBI, says it detected no access to its models, its code or its customers' data. The company adds that its own models helped identify the suspect.

items.titre: American Express and Shopify equip AI agents to buy
items.texteHtml: American Express presented a framework on Tuesday 13 October meant to stop an AI agent (a program that carries out tasks end to end) from buying anything other than what its holder authorised. The point, according to TechCrunch, is to avoid mistaken purchases and disputes as AI-driven buying spreads. The same day, Shopify opened its catalogue, more than a billion listings, to more agents: a customer will be able to set up their assistant to order on their behalf. The two announcements sketch the same economy, called agentic, where the software places the order itself. For a procurement department or an IT department, the question becomes one of mandate, what an agent can commit to on its own and up to what amount.

items.titre: Chinese chip exports jump 136% to $45 billion
items.texteHtml: Chinese exports of integrated circuits rose 136% year on year in September, to $45 billion, according to customs data cited by the South China Morning Post. The increase outpaces the 108% rate recorded over the first nine months of the year. By volume, China exported only 1% more chips (32.7 billion units): it is the price surge, driven by the memory shortage, that explains the leap in value. The country confirms its growing weight in the global semiconductor chain, despite American export controls.

items.titre: Memory-chip makers' shares fall in Asia
items.texteHtml: The shares of Asian memory-chip makers dropped sharply this week, a sign of growing doubts about how long the AI-driven profit cycle will last, the South China Morning Post reports. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell 7.4% and 10.1% on Tuesday, dragging down China's CXMT (ChangXin Memory Technologies) as well. The paradox is stark: memory prices are rising and quarterly results stay solid, but investors are questioning a possible turn. The two movements, sharply rising exports and falling shares, tell the same tension around a memory market boosted by AI demand.

items.titre: The debate over the risks of open models hardens
items.texteHtml: Should the most powerful models be opened up? MIT Technology Review devotes a feature to the benefits and risks of open-weight models (which you can download and run yourself). The debate flared up after a report from Anthropic claiming that a model from China's Z.ai, GLM, poses a serious cyberattack risk. On Tuesday, an Anthropic commercial executive repeated to Bloomberg that open models carry "more risk" of security incidents. Wired, for its part, reports that a model with its safeguards removed readily provides detailed instructions for making an explosive device. The feature comes as the European AI Act seeks to distinguish what counts as open source from what requires heightened oversight.

items.titre: ASML raises its forecasts, unable to keep up with demand
items.texteHtml: The Dutch firm ASML, a critical link in chip manufacturing, raised its annual sales forecast to €44-45 billion and is seeking to produce more lithography machines, lifted by AI spending.

items.titre: The New York Times, AFP and 80 media outlets unite against AI
items.texteHtml: The New York Times, The Economist and AFP are joining SPUR, a coalition of nearly 80 news organisations across more than 20 countries, to govern AI access to their content and negotiate licences.

items.titre: Google gives AI agents an ID card in Workspace
items.texteHtml: Google now requires AI agents that access its office suite to be declared and assigns them their own identity; in many companies, the agent still works under an employee's account.

analyse.titre: AI agents start to pay and to access: the question becomes under which identity
analyse.these: AI agents are starting to pay and to access systems, often under an employee's account; before you let them act, give them their own identity, bounded rights and a record of what they do.
analyse.html:
American Express published a framework on Tuesday that stops an AI agent from buying anything other than what its user authorised. The same day, Shopify opened its catalogue, more than a billion listings, to those same agents so they can place orders on our behalf, and Google began requiring every organisation to declare the agents that access Workspace, its office suite. Three moves, one shift: the AI agent is starting to act. It pays, it accesses, it commits.

We note that this movement shifts the question of AI at work. For two years, it held in one sentence: what can the model produce. It now holds in another: under which identity did the agent act. In most French organisations, an agent plugged into the ERP or the email system borrows an employee's account. When it sends a purchase order, edits a customer record or reads an inbox, the record bears the name of a person who did nothing. On the day of a dispute, a CNIL inspection or an incident, no one can say who, the human or the machine, performed the act.

The move that protects fits in one line: before letting an agent act, give it its own identity, not a colleague's badge. The Journal du Net puts it well: an AI agent is not a service account inherited from the 1990s. Each agent deserves a named identity, permissions bounded to its task, a log of its actions. This can be learned and organised: map the agents already in service, decide who has the right to create them, set what they can commit to on their own and what requires human approval.

GDPR officers know the principle: it is controller accountability. It changes scale when the actor becomes a program that decides on its own, thousands of times a day. Amex and Shopify have just equipped agents to spend. Your teams will use them. What remains is to decide under whose name they will sign.

The Masteria editorial team.
